/itineraryStops/2/smartNotes/facilities.source_en: Tourist Information Center near Anguk Station Exit 2 with multilingual maps. Coffee shops, traditional teahouses, hanok-converted cafes scattered through the village. Photo zones marked.

/itineraryStops/2/whyOnRoute.source_en: Bukchon is the natural pivot from Gyeongbokgung's grand-scale royal architecture to a domestic-scale Joseon-era streetscape — completing the 'how kings AND aristocrats lived 500 years ago' narrative within walking distance. Picked over Namsangol Hanok Village (a curated open-air museum) because Bukchon is a LIVING village with residents — far more authentic for the story-driven cruise passenger window. For cruise guests on a one-day-in-Seoul window, Bukchon delivers the day's strongest 'period-set' photo opportunity — hanok rooflines + ⟦G0⟧-bound alley vistas + the Bukchon 8 Gyeong viewpoints make this a 75-min Instagram-grade stop within walking distance of both Gyeongbokgung and ⟦G0⟧.

/itineraryStops/2/convenience/restroom.source_en: Tourist Information Center at Bukchon entrance; cafes scattered through the village

/itineraryStops/2/description.source_en:
Bukchon literally means 'Northern Village' — a 600-year-old hanok (traditional Korean tile-roofed house) residential district nestled between ⟦G1⟧ and Changdeokgung Palace, originally home to high-ranking Joseon Dynasty government officials and aristocracy. 

Today Bukchon is Seoul's largest concentration of preserved hanok homes — approximately 900 traditional houses arrayed along eight famous viewpoints (Bukchon 8 Gyeong / Bukchon 8 Views) — with sloping alleys giving views of N Seoul Tower in the distance and the curved tile-roof rooflines layering down toward the city below. 

The signature view is Gye-dong-gil (Hanok Roofline Alley near Bukchon No. 6 viewpoint) where photographers gather for the iconic shot of cascading hanok rooftops with N Seoul Tower in the distance. Many hanok along the route are private residences (residents have asked tourists to stay quiet — the busiest residential Red Zone now restricts tourist entry from 17:00 to 10:00 the next day, with fines enforced from March 2025). 

Cultural workshops scattered through the village offer hands-on experiences in Korean knot-tying, hanji (mulberry paper) crafts, traditional tea ceremonies, embroidery, and Korean cooking. Hanbok rental shops cluster at the village edge (~15,000-20,000 KRW for 4 hours) — the standard photo-trip pairing with Gyeongbokgung. 

⟦G2⟧, the cultural and crafts shopping street, sits a 5-10 minute walk south. The village's preservation is overseen by **Jongno-gu District Office's ⟦G0⟧ preservation program** — strict zoning rules limit commercial signage, renovation must use traditional materials (handmade hanji paper screens, wooden frames, tile roofs), and the Red Zone entry restriction from 17:00 to 10:00 is enforced by signage and community wardens during peak season.

/itineraryStops/3/highlights/7.source_en: **Anthony Bourdain's 'Parts Unknown' Seoul episode (CNN, June 21, 2015)** + **Netflix 'Street Food: Asia' (2019)** = catapulted Gwangjang to international food-pilgrimage status; pre-Bourdain it was a working-class market unknown to international tourists

/itineraryStops/3/highlights/8.source_en: **General market 09:00–18:00** (textile + hanbok-fabric + traditional dry goods upper level) **/ Food alley 09:00–23:00** (most stalls 11:00 onward) — Sundays + holidays see lighter crowds for early-bird visits

/itineraryStops/3/smartNotes/tip.source_en: **Bring CASH 10,000-20,000 KRW per person.** Try bindaetteok + mayak gimbap as the must-eat pair. Avoid seasoning samples without intent to purchase (Korean market etiquette). Visit before 12:00 OR after 14:00 to skip peak crowds. Yukhoe (raw beef) is safe — vendors source same-day fresh — but skip if you're sensitive to raw foods. Pair the food alley with the second-floor textile district if you want a Korean wedding hanbok souvenir.

/itineraryStops/3/smartNotes/facilities.source_en: Many vendors have small sit-down dining areas behind their stalls. Multilingual menu boards. Some now accept cards but assume cash-only. ATMs near Jongno 5-ga Station Exit 7.

/itineraryStops/3/whyOnRoute.source_en: Gwangjang is Seoul's most authentic non-tourist food experience — a working-class market that international media made world-famous without it losing its character. Picked over Namdaemun Market (larger but more Chinese-tour-bus dominated) because Gwangjang's food alley is a single covered ribbon perfect for a 75-min lunch stop — the alley's compact layout means cruise passengers see a dozen specialties in a single pass, eat at one or two counters, and leave full. For cruise guests, the 75-min Gwangjang lunch slot is the day's most cost-efficient meal — bindaetteok + mayak gimbap + tteokbokki for ~10,000-15,000 KRW per person vs ~25,000-40,000 KRW for a comparable ⟦G0⟧ sit-down lunch.

/itineraryStops/3/convenience/parking.source_en: Limited; nearest paid parking ~5 min walk
